query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a vapor-deposited interlayer (e.g., a thin nickel coating) on tungsten particles will improve copper wettability during spark plasma sintering, thus reducing interfacial voids and phase separation, and ultimately enhancing both thermal transport and mechanical durability compared to composites made with uncoated W particles.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite precursor consisting of tungsten particles dispersed in a copper matrix (or mixed with Cu powders) without any surface modification.
generation.intervention: Introduce a vapor-deposited interlayer (such as a thin Ni coating) on the surfaces of tungsten particles prior to spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Spark plasma sintering conducted at temperatures below tungsten’s melting point, under pressures and hold times typical for fabricating W–Cu composites, ensuring that the coating remains intact and effective during processing.
generation.structural_mediator: An enhanced W–Cu interfacial region with improved wettability provided by the interlayer, leading to a reduction of voids and a more uniform distribution of constituents.
generation.mechanism: The vapor-deposited interlayer modifies the surface energy of tungsten particles, enhancing Cu wetting during sintering. This improved wetting minimizes the formation of voids and phase separation, producing better contact at the metal–metal interface and preserving mechanical durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite should exhibit a more uniform microstructure with fewer voids and defects, resulting in improved thermal conductivity and mechanical integrity relative to composites produced from uncoated W particles.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites fabricated by conventional spark plasma sintering or metal 3D printing methods using uncoated tungsten particles.
generation.boundary: The intervention is limited to processing conditions where sintering temperatures remain well below the melting point of tungsten, and the interlayer deposition does not compromise the inherent high-temperature stability and mechanical robustness of the composite.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvements in thermal transport and mechanical durability is not precisely predicted. In addition, the optimal thickness and composition of the interlayer require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples via spark plasma sintering under identical processing conditions: one set using tungsten particles with a vapor-deposited Ni interlayer and a control set with uncoated tungsten particles. Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, X-ray tomography) and property measurements will be performed.
measurements: Void density and interfacial contact quality via high-resolution imaging
Mechanical durability tests (such as flexural or compression strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in void density and an improvement in thermal conductivity and mechanical strength compared to the uncoated control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

reading.lever: Introduce a vapor-deposited interlayer (or coat) on W particles to enhance Cu wettability during SPS.
reading.why: This surface-coating strategy, successful in achieving near-perfect interparticle contact in thin film systems, directly addresses void and phase separation issues while preserving mechanical durability in W–Cu composites.
